title: Asset types: four ways a building earns its money
summary: A rental earns rent under leases, a condominium earns a one-time profit on sale, a hotel earns nightly revenue as an operating business, and mixed-use combines streams that must be valued separately. Each has its own metrics, its own risks and its own buyer. Choosing the asset type is choosing the business you are in.
body:
Mr Shabazz, the same concrete frame can be four different businesses. A rental collects rent under leases, a condominium sells once and leaves, a hotel sells a night at a time and runs an operating company, and a mixed-use building does several of these at once. Choose the asset type and you have chosen your risks, your metrics and your eventual buyer.

Recall

Q. From feasibility, what is a reliance letter?

A. An agreement letting a named third party, such as a lender, rely on a consultant’s report, usually on the original terms and liability limits. Negotiate it before the report is delivered.

Q. From cycles, why do property markets overshoot?

A. Because of the supply lag: developers react to the same strong rents together, and their buildings deliver years later, together, often into a weaker market.

Q. From liability, what does limited liability protect, and what can defeat it?

A. It limits a shareholder’s loss to what they invested in the company. Courts can set it aside in narrow cases, often described as piercing the corporate veil, typically where the company was used as a sham or to commit fraud; the tests vary by jurisdiction.

Why this matters

Remi here. Developers often choose an asset type by looking at which one shows the highest number in a spreadsheet. That is backwards. Each asset type is a different business, with a different relationship to the cycle, a different lender appetite and a different exit buyer. A developer who understands that can match the product to the site, the market and his own balance sheet, rather than to the most exciting projection.

Rental and condominium: rent forever, or profit once

In plain English, a rental building is owned as a whole and its units are leased. Income arrives monthly, the owner keeps the building and the value comes from the net operating income (NOI), the rent collected minus operating costs, divided by a cap rate. A condominium building is divided into individually owned units sold to buyers. The developer earns a profit on sale and, once the units close, has no income stream and usually no ongoing interest.

The professional framing is that a rental is a long-duration income asset whose risk is lease-up, operating cost and exit cap rate, while a condominium is a short-duration trading business whose risk is sales pace, buyer closing and construction cost. A rental needs patient capital and long debt. A condominium can return capital faster but usually depends on pre-sales to secure construction financing, which ties its fate to the buyers’ ability to close.

Worked example one, with hypothetical numbers. A 100-unit building costs $40,000,000. As a rental, units rent at an average of $2,000 a month. Gross potential rent is 100 times $2,000 times 12, which is $2,400,000 a year. With 5 percent vacancy and operating costs of $750,000, NOI is about $1,530,000, a yield on cost of about 3.8 percent. That is thin in most markets. As a condominium, the same units sell at an average of $480,000, for $48,000,000 of revenue. After selling costs of 5 percent, about $45,600,000, a profit of $5,600,000 on cost. The condominium looks better here, but the rental would still be owned, earning income, ten years later. The comparison is never just one number against another.

Hotel: a business that happens to be a building

A hotel sells a room for a night, every night, and the price changes with demand. That makes it an operating business, with staff, a brand, distribution costs and daily revenue management. Three terms run hotel conversations. Average daily rate (ADR) is rooms revenue divided by room nights sold: the average price actually paid per occupied room. Occupancy is room nights sold divided by room nights available. Revenue per available room (RevPAR) is rooms revenue divided by room nights available, which equals ADR times occupancy. RevPAR matters because it captures price and volume together: a hotel can raise ADR by turning guests away, and RevPAR will show whether that was wise.

Worked example two, hypothetical. A 100-room hotel achieves an ADR of $150 at 70 percent occupancy. RevPAR is $150 times 0.70, which is $105. Rooms revenue for the year is 100 rooms times 365 nights times $105, about $3,830,000. Compare it with the rental’s $2,400,000 of gross potential rent: the hotel’s revenue is far higher. But a hotel’s operating costs are also far higher, often well over half of revenue, and they include labour that cannot be cut quickly when demand falls. What matters is the profit after running the business, which hotel accounts call gross operating profit (GOP): total revenue minus the costs of operating the hotel, before management fees, fixed charges and reserves.

Say that out loud now.

Apart-hotel and mixed-use: hybrids with their own rules

An apart-hotel, sometimes called serviced apartments, rents furnished units with kitchens for stays of days to months. It usually runs at higher occupancy and lower ADR than a full-service hotel, with lighter staffing and little or no restaurant. It sits between a rental and a hotel in risk and reward, and in many places between them in regulation, which affects zoning, building code occupancy classification and tax treatment. A mixed-use building combines uses, such as retail at grade, offices or a hotel above, and apartments at the top. Each component has its own income, its own cap rate and its own buyer, and the shared parts of the building, such as structure, cores and parking, must be allocated among them by agreement.

Matching the product to the site

A professional asks three questions before choosing. What does this location’s demand actually want: households staying years, buyers wanting to own, or visitors staying nights? What will lenders finance here, for this product, at what leverage? And who buys the finished asset? A site near a business district with strong weekday travel and weak family demand may suit a hotel or apart-hotel; the same land in a growing suburb may suit rentals. The site and the market choose the asset type more often than the developer does.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is choosing the asset type for its headline revenue rather than for the business it puts you in. The control is to compare asset types on NOI, value, capital required, time to return of capital and behaviour in a downturn, side by side, before the design is fixed.

The beginner’s mistake

The beginner compares a hotel’s revenue with a rental’s rent and concludes the hotel is better. The professional compares what each produces after the cost of running it, and then asks which one a lender will finance and a buyer will buy at the end.

Six-Lens Check

Tax: income from operating a hotel may be treated differently from rental income, and a condominium sale may be treated as business income rather than a capital gain; verify that against the primary source before you rely on it. Liability: a hotel brings guest safety, employment and food service liabilities that a rental does not. Banking: lenders apply different coverage ratios and loan sizes to each asset type, and hotels usually get less leverage. Governance: a hotel needs an owner who can supervise an operator; a condominium hands governance to a unit-owner corporation. Estate: a rental is a long-term asset that can pass to heirs; a hotel is a business that needs active management after you. Exit: each type has a different buyer pool, so decide who buys before you design.

Callback

In Week 10 you learned that value is NOI divided by the cap rate. This week adds that each asset type earns its NOI differently and trades at a different cap rate, because buyers price the stability of the income. And in Week 27 you saw that hotels sit closest to the cycle: room rates can change every night, so they move first in a downturn and first in a recovery.

Recap

Rentals earn lease income and are valued on NOI. Condominiums earn a one-time profit on sale. Hotels are operating businesses measured by ADR, occupancy, RevPAR and GOP. Apart-hotels and mixed-use are hybrids with their own rules. Choose the business, not the headline.

Next: Ford, Failure Forensics — Stuyvesant Town, where a residential asset was bought for income its rules did not allow.
checklist: Compare asset types on NOI, value, capital, time to return of capital and downturn behaviour.
Calculate RevPAR as ADR times occupancy, and check it against rooms revenue.
Compare a hotel with a rental on profit after operating costs, never on revenue.
Identify the likely exit buyer for each asset type before design is fixed.
Check how zoning, building code and tax classify an apart-hotel in your jurisdiction.
List the shared elements of a mixed-use building and how each will be allocated.
Ask lenders for indicative loan sizes for each asset type early.
head: Field checklist
speak: The same building can be four different businesses. A rental leases units and is valued on net operating income. A condominium sells units once and leaves, so its risk is sales pace and closing. A hotel sells a room a night at a time, so it is an operating business. Three terms run it: average daily rate, the price paid per occupied room; occupancy, the share of rooms sold; and revenue per available room, which is the two multiplied. A hypothetical 100-room hotel at 150 dollars and 70 percent occupancy has a RevPAR of 105 dollars and about 3.8 million of rooms revenue, far more than a rental’s 2.4 million of rent. But hotel costs are much higher, so what matters is gross operating profit after running the business. Apart-hotels and mixed-use are hybrids. I choose the business, its lender and its buyer, not the headline revenue.
terms: Average daily rate (ADR) — rooms revenue divided by room nights sold; the average price paid per occupied room.
Revenue per available room (RevPAR) — rooms revenue divided by room nights available, equal to ADR times occupancy.
Gross operating profit (GOP) — a hotel’s total revenue minus operating costs, before management fees, fixed charges and reserves.

hostile.q: Your hotel produces twice the revenue of the apartment scheme. Why should I lend more against it?
hostile.a: You should not, on revenue. On net operating income after fees, fixed charges and the furniture reserve, the hotel is roughly comparable, and its income is more volatile. I am asking you to lend on the stabilised net income at a hotel coverage ratio, which is why the loan request is lower than the apartment scheme’s.

role: Failure forensics, with Roman assisting on finance
title: Stuyvesant Town 2006–2010: buying income the rules did not allow
summary: In 2006 a venture bought Stuyvesant Town–Peter Cooper Village, a large rent-regulated Manhattan complex, for about 5.4 billion dollars, on a plan to move apartments to market rents. Conversions came more slowly than planned, a 2009 court ruling went against the strategy, the reserves funding the gap ran down, and in 2010 the owners handed the property to lenders. The root cause was debt sized on income the asset type and its rules did not yet allow.
body:
Mr Shabazz, Stuyvesant Town shows what happens when an asset is bought for the income it might earn once its rules change, rather than the income it actually earns under the rules it has. The buildings were sound and the location was excellent. The business plan was the problem.

Recall

Q. From this week, what is RevPAR?

A. Revenue per available room: rooms revenue divided by room nights available, equal to average daily rate times occupancy.

Q. From cycles, what is Rule 27?

A. Fund long projects with long money, never let a refinancing date fall where a downturn can reach it unprotected, and never let one project grow larger than the balance sheet can carry through the worst year of the last cycle.

Q. From liability, what is agency?

A. A relationship in which one person, the agent, is authorised to act for another, the principal, and can bind the principal to contracts within that authority.

Why this matters

Ford here, with Roman assisting on the finance. Residential property is usually thought of as the safest asset type. This case shows that safety depends on reading the rules that govern the income. Rent regulation, tax incentives and tenant protections are part of the asset, just as the concrete is. A buyer who treats them as obstacles to be removed, rather than facts to be priced, is underwriting a change in the law. This lesson stays with the broad public record; where details are contested we avoid them.

Step 1: Timeline

Stuyvesant Town and Peter Cooper Village is a large complex of apartment buildings in Manhattan, with roughly 11,000 apartments, built after the Second World War and long owned by the insurer MetLife. Most of its apartments were rent-stabilised under New York’s rent rules, which limit rent increases for existing tenants. In 2006 MetLife sold the complex to a venture led by Tishman Speyer and BlackRock for about $5.4 billion, widely reported as one of the largest residential property sales in American history. The plan relied on increasing income by moving apartments to market rents as they turned over. The purchase was funded with a large senior mortgage and several layers of subordinate debt, with reserves set aside to cover the expected gap between income and debt service while rents rose. In 2009 New York’s highest court ruled, in a case brought by tenants, that apartments in buildings receiving a particular property tax benefit could not be taken out of rent stabilisation while that benefit was being received. Income growth fell far behind the plan, the reserves ran down, and in early 2010 the owners defaulted and handed control of the property to its lenders. The complex was later sold to new owners.

Step 2: Key decisions

Three decisions mattered. Paying a price that only made sense if regulated rents moved substantially toward market levels. Funding that price with high leverage across several layers of debt. And relying on reserves to carry the property until the projected income arrived, rather than sizing the debt to the income that existed.

Step 3: Assumptions

The core assumption was that apartments would turn over and convert to market rent at a planned pace. The second was that the rules permitting those conversions would remain as the buyers read them. The third was that the market for rents and for refinancing would stay strong long enough for the plan to work. All three depended on events outside the owners’ control.

Say that out loud now.

Step 4: Incentives

The sale was competitive, which rewarded the bidder willing to assume the most rent growth. Lenders in 2006 were packaging loans into securities and selling them on, which reduced their incentive to question projected income. Debt and equity investors were attracted by the scale and prestige of the asset. Tenants, by contrast, had every incentive to resist the business plan, and the law gave them tools to do so.

Step 5: Warning signs ignored

Rent stabilisation and the tax-benefit question were known features of the property, and tenant groups opposed the strategy from the start. A plan that depends on existing tenants leaving, in a city with strong tenant protections, has a natural speed limit. And by 2007 and 2008 credit markets were tightening, which made the reserves and refinancing assumptions more fragile.

Step 6: Point of no return

The point of no return was the closing in 2006, when a price and a debt load that required regulated income to become market income were locked in. After that, the owners could only win if conversions ran on schedule and the legal reading held. The 2009 ruling and the downturn removed both.

Step 7: Root cause

Roman’s summary: the root cause was debt sized on income the asset type and its rules did not yet allow. A residential asset with regulated rents was financed as if it were a market-rent asset in waiting. The reserves did not fix that; they only measured how long the hope could last.

What the underwriting should have asked

Roman again. Picture yourself as a lender reviewing the deal in 2006. Four questions would have exposed most of the risk without hindsight. What does the property earn today, under today’s rules, and what loan does that income support at a normal coverage ratio? How many apartments turn over each year in practice, not in the plan? Which legal questions affect whether a vacant apartment can move to market rent, and what is counsel’s view of each? And how many months do the reserves last if conversions run at half the planned pace? A deal that needs all four answers to come out favourably is a deal that needs luck.

The small-developer version

This is a composite example. A developer buys an older 40-unit rental building whose rents are well below market, planning to renovate units as tenants leave and re-let them at higher rents. With hypothetical numbers: current NOI is $400,000, the plan projects $700,000 within three years, and the loan is sized on $600,000 with an interest reserve covering the gap. Tenants stay longer than expected, local rules limit increases on renovated units, and after three years NOI is $480,000. The reserve is gone, the loan matures and the refinance supports only a fraction of the balance. It is Stuyvesant Town at one three-hundredth of the scale.

One more observation from the public record. The case is often told as a story about a downturn, but the downturn only shortened the timeline. Even in a strong market, a plan that needs thousands of regulated tenants to leave on schedule is a plan with a speed limit set by other people’s choices.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is underwriting a change in rules, tenants or market as if it were already income. The control: size debt to current income under current rules, treat projected increases as upside funded with equity, and get written legal advice on every rule the plan depends on.

The beginner’s mistake

The beginner reads below-market rents as an opportunity and stops there. The professional asks why they are below market, what law keeps them there and how fast that has ever changed in practice.

Callback

In Week 24 you learned that substance outweighs form when a tax authority reviews a transaction. Here the same idea worked through tenancy law: the substance of the asset was regulated housing, whatever the business plan called it. And in Week 21 you met limited liability: the owners’ loss was largely limited to their equity because the debt sat in property companies, which is exactly how ring-fencing is meant to work.

Recap

A large rent-regulated complex was bought on the assumption that regulated rents would become market rents. Conversions were slow, a court ruling went against the plan and the reserves ran out. Rule 29 follows from it.

Rule 29: Underwrite the income the asset type and its rules allow today, and never size debt on income you can only earn by changing the tenants, the law or the market.

Next: Sage, The Money — how each asset type turns income into value, and why a hotel’s revenue is not its value.
checklist: Value every acquisition on current income under current rules first.
Size debt to that income at a normal coverage ratio.
Treat projected rent increases as upside funded with equity, not with debt.
Measure actual unit turnover from history, not from the plan.
Get written legal advice on every rule the business plan depends on.
Calculate how long reserves last at half the planned pace.
Run the seven steps on any asset-type failure you study.
head: Field checklist
rule: Rule 29: Underwrite the income the asset type and its rules allow today, and never size debt on income you can only earn by changing the tenants, the law or the market.
speak: Stuyvesant Town and Peter Cooper Village is a complex of about 11,000 apartments in Manhattan, mostly rent-stabilised. In 2006 a venture led by Tishman Speyer and BlackRock bought it from MetLife for about 5.4 billion dollars, planning to move apartments to market rents as tenants left. It was financed with layers of debt and reserves to cover the gap until income rose. Conversions ran slowly, tenants resisted, and in 2009 New York’s highest court ruled that apartments in buildings receiving a certain tax benefit could not be deregulated. The reserves ran down and in early 2010 the owners handed the property to lenders. The point of no return was the 2006 closing. The root cause was debt sized on income the rules did not yet allow. My rule: underwrite the income the asset and its rules allow today, and never size debt on income I can only earn by changing the tenants, the law or the market.
terms: Rent stabilisation — a legal regime that limits rent increases for existing tenants and protects their right to renew.
Interest reserve — cash set aside at closing to pay interest while a property’s income is below what the debt requires.
Value-add plan — a business plan that raises income through renovation, re-leasing or repositioning after purchase.

hostile.q: Your plan raises rents 40 percent in three years. What happens to my loan if they rise 10 percent?
hostile.a: Nothing that threatens it. The loan is sized on today’s income at your coverage ratio; the rent increase is funded with our equity and is upside only. If rents rise 10 percent, our return falls and your coverage improves slightly. Counsel’s written view on every rule the plan depends on is in the pack.

title: From revenue to value: why a hotel’s revenue is not its worth
summary: Each asset type turns revenue into value through a different chain. A rental’s NOI is capitalised at a low cap rate; a hotel must pay its operator, its fixed charges and a furniture reserve before reaching NOI, and is then capitalised at a higher rate. A condominium has no NOI at all; it is judged on profit margin and speed. Higher revenue can mean lower value.
body:
Mr Shabazz, revenue is where the asset-type comparison starts and the place where most bad decisions are made. Follow each type from revenue all the way to value, and the building with the biggest top line often ends up worth less.

Recall

Q. From this week, what was the root cause at Stuyvesant Town?

A. Debt sized on income the asset type and its rules did not yet allow: regulated housing financed as if it were market-rent housing in waiting.

Q. From cycles, through what three channels does a rate rise reach your equity?

A. The loan the income supports shrinks, value falls as cap rates rise, and floating-rate debt costs more.

Q. From liability, what is negligence in concept?

A. A failure to take the care a reasonable person would take, where a duty of care is owed, causing foreseeable loss. The elements and tests vary by jurisdiction.

Why this matters

Sage here. Every asset type has a revenue line, an expense line and a value, but the steps between them differ. If you skip a step, you overvalue the asset, borrow too much against it and price your exit wrongly. Today we walk the chain for a rental, a hotel and a condominium using hypothetical round numbers, and you will see why lenders and buyers treat them so differently.

The rental chain

In plain English: rent comes in, vacancy and operating costs come out, and what remains is the net operating income (NOI). A buyer capitalises that NOI at a cap rate that reflects how stable it is. Apartments with many tenants on staggered leases have stable income, so they usually trade at relatively low cap rates.

Worked example one, hypothetical. A 120-unit rental collects gross potential rent of $2,880,000 a year, at $2,000 a month per unit. Vacancy and bad debt of 5 percent removes $144,000. Operating costs, including property tax, insurance, repairs, utilities and management, are $900,000. NOI is $1,836,000. At a 5.5 percent cap rate, value is $1,836,000 divided by 0.055, about $33,400,000. NOI is about 64 percent of gross rent.

The hotel chain

A hotel’s chain has more links. Total revenue includes rooms, food and beverage and other income. Departmental costs, such as housekeeping and kitchen, and undistributed costs, such as sales, administration, energy and repairs, are deducted to reach gross operating profit (GOP). Then the owner pays the operator a base management fee, usually a percentage of revenue, and often an incentive fee, usually a percentage of profit. Then come fixed charges, such as property tax and insurance. Finally, a reserve for replacing furniture, fixtures and equipment, called the FF&E reserve, set aside as a percentage of revenue because rooms wear out on a short cycle. What remains is the hotel’s NOI. Fee and reserve percentages are commercial practice negotiated in each management agreement, not standards.

Worked example two, hypothetical. A 120-room hotel produces total revenue of $6,300,000. GOP at a 35 percent margin is about $2,200,000. Base fee at 3 percent of revenue is about $190,000. Incentive fee at 8 percent of GOP is about $176,000. Fixed charges are $300,000. FF&E reserve at 4 percent of revenue is about $252,000. NOI is roughly $1,290,000, about 20 percent of revenue. A buyer applies a higher cap rate, say 8.5 percent, because hotel income moves with every night’s demand. Value is about $15,200,000.

Put the two side by side. The hotel’s revenue of $6,300,000 is more than twice the rental’s $2,880,000. Its value of about $15,200,000 is less than half of the rental’s $33,400,000. Same number of keys, same land, more staff, more risk, less value.

Say that out loud now.

The condominium chain

A condominium has no NOI and no cap rate. Revenue is the sum of unit sales. From it come selling costs and the full development cost, and what remains is profit. The professional measures are profit as a percentage of cost or of revenue, and how quickly capital comes back. Worked example three, hypothetical: 120 units sell at an average of $420,000, revenue of $50,400,000. Selling and marketing at 5 percent is $2,520,000. Development cost is $40,000,000. Profit is $7,880,000, about 20 percent on cost. The developer’s capital is back within months of completion, but only if buyers close, which is the risk you studied in Week 28.

How the best do it

Experienced hotel owners typically separate owning a hotel from operating it, and employ an asset manager who works for the owner and watches the operator: reviewing the annual budget, comparing performance with a set of competing hotels and enforcing the management agreement. What a small developer can copy is the habit of measuring the operator against a defined competitive set, using RevPAR index, which is your hotel’s RevPAR divided by the competitive set’s, rather than against the operator’s own budget.

Wealth Ledger

Warrick’s note. On your personal balance sheet, these assets behave differently. A stabilised rental is a long-term income asset, relatively easy to borrow against. A hotel is closer to owning an operating company, with income that can fall sharply in a downturn and is harder to sell quickly. A condominium project is a trading position that becomes cash, which then needs a new home. Decide which mix supports your liquidity floor, and do not hold more volatile income than your reserves can carry for a bad year.

The mixed-use chain

A mixed-use building is valued component by component, because buyers price each income stream separately. Worked example four, hypothetical. A building has ground-floor retail earning NOI of $400,000 and apartments above earning $1,500,000. Retail income depends on a few tenants and is priced at a 6.5 percent cap rate, giving about $6,150,000. Apartment income is priced at 5.5 percent, giving about $27,300,000. Total value is about $33,450,000. Had you capitalised the combined $1,900,000 at the apartment rate, you would have shown about $34,550,000, overstating value by about $1,100,000 because the retail was priced as if it were apartments.

The second issue in mixed-use is cost allocation. Shared elements, such as the structure, cores, roof, parking and building systems, must be split between components, both for the pro forma and for the eventual legal documents if the components are ever sold separately. An allocation that loads shared costs onto the component you plan to sell first can flatter its margin and starve the one you keep. Decide the allocation rule early, write it down and apply it consistently.

A lender will do the same arithmetic and will usually size the loan component by component as well, often lending less against the retail than against the apartments. So the component split is not an accounting nicety; it decides the loan, the value and the order in which you can sell.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is valuing a hotel or apart-hotel on revenue, or on GOP, instead of on NOI after fees, fixed charges and the FF&E reserve. The control: run every asset type through its full chain to NOI and apply the cap rate buyers use for that type, not the one used for apartments.

The beginner’s mistake

The beginner leaves out the FF&E reserve because it is not an expense paid every month. The professional treats it as a real cost, because the rooms will need refurbishing on schedule whether or not anyone saved for it.

Callback

In Week 14 you built a rental pro forma from revenue through vacancy and operating costs to stabilised NOI. The hotel chain is the same idea with more deductions and a different cap rate. And in Week 16 you met appraiser bias: hotel valuations are especially sensitive to the operator’s projections, so ask whose numbers they are.

Recap

A rental capitalises NOI at a low rate. A hotel deducts management fees, fixed charges and a furniture reserve before NOI, then uses a higher cap rate. A condominium is judged on profit margin and speed of return. The biggest revenue can produce the smallest value.

Next: LEX, The Rules — the contracts and statutes behind each asset type, and how Canada and Guyana approach them.
checklist: Run every asset type from revenue all the way to NOI or profit.
Deduct hotel base and incentive fees, fixed charges and the FF&E reserve before NOI.
Apply the cap rate buyers use for each asset type, not one rate for all.
Judge a condominium on profit on cost and speed of return of capital.
Measure a hotel operator by RevPAR index against a defined competitive set.
Ask whose projections a hotel valuation relies on.
Record volatile hotel income at a stressed level on your personal balance sheet.
head: Field checklist
speak: Each asset type turns revenue into value differently. A hypothetical 120-unit rental collects 2.88 million of rent; after vacancy and 900,000 of operating costs, NOI is about 1.84 million, worth about 33.4 million at a 5.5 percent cap rate. A 120-room hotel earns 6.3 million of revenue, more than twice as much. But after operating costs its gross operating profit is about 2.2 million, and after the base and incentive management fees, 300,000 of fixed charges and a 4 percent furniture reserve, NOI is about 1.29 million. Buyers capitalise hotel income at a higher rate, say 8.5 percent, so it is worth about 15.2 million, less than half the rental. A condominium has no NOI at all; it is judged on profit on cost and how fast the capital comes back. The biggest revenue can produce the smallest value.
terms: FF&E reserve — money set aside from hotel revenue to replace furniture, fixtures and equipment on a regular cycle.
Incentive management fee — a fee paid to a hotel operator based on profit, usually above a threshold.
RevPAR index — a hotel’s RevPAR divided by the RevPAR of its competitive set, showing whether it wins or loses share.

hostile.q: Your hotel shows 2.2 million of gross operating profit. Why are you valuing it on 1.29 million?
hostile.a: Because you would. Gross operating profit is before the operator’s fees, property tax, insurance and the furniture reserve, and all four will be paid. NOI after them is 1.29 million, and at a hotel cap rate that is what a buyer will pay for.

title: The legal form of each asset type: lease, declaration, management agreement
summary: Each asset type rests on a different legal instrument: residential tenancy law for rentals, a condominium statute and declaration for condominiums, a hotel management agreement for hotels, and a mix for apart-hotels and mixed-use. A condo-hotel rental programme can also raise securities questions. Read the instrument before you choose the product.
body:
Mr Shabazz, every asset type is a legal structure before it is a building. A rental lives under tenancy law, a condominium under a statute and a declaration, a hotel under a management agreement, and the hybrids under several at once. Choose the product without reading those instruments, and you have signed up to rules you never priced.

Recall

Q. From this week, why is a hotel with more revenue often worth less than a rental?

A. Because a hotel pays high operating costs, management fees, fixed charges and a furniture reserve before reaching NOI, and buyers then apply a higher cap rate to its more volatile income.

Q. From cycles, how can you be in breach of a loan without missing a payment?

A. Through a covenant, such as a loan-to-value limit, that trips when a new appraisal shows a lower value.

Q. From liability, what does piercing the corporate veil mean?

A. A court disregarding the separate existence of a company to hold its owners liable, usually only in narrow cases such as fraud or sham arrangements.

Why this matters

LEX here. When developers compare asset types, they compare numbers. The legal instruments behind each type decide whether those numbers can be earned and kept. A rental’s rent is capped by whatever tenancy law allows. A condominium’s profit depends on the statute governing deposits and disclosure. A hotel’s income passes through an operator whose agreement may be very hard to end. These are not details for closing; they shape the product.

Rentals and condominiums

In plain English, residential tenancy law governs the relationship between a landlord and a residential tenant: how rent can rise, how a tenancy ends, what notice is required and what repairs the landlord owes. In many places it overrides the lease, so a clause the tenant signed may not be enforceable. A condominium is created under a condominium statute by registering a declaration, the founding document that divides the building into units and common elements and sets each unit’s share of common expenses and votes. The statute usually also regulates deposits, the disclosure buyers must receive and the developer’s duties during the turnover to the owners’ corporation.

The professional framing is that tenancy law and condominium law are largely mandatory: you can add terms, but you usually cannot contract out of the protections. Read them as fixed parameters of the product.

Hotels: the management agreement

Most owners do not run their own hotels. They sign a hotel management agreement with an operator, often attached to a brand, under which the operator runs the hotel in the owner’s name and at the owner’s cost, for fees. The agreement sets the term, the fees, the owner’s approval rights over budgets and key staff, the brand standards the owner must fund, and the conditions on which either side can end it. Termination rights are usually the most important and most negotiated clause.

Worked example one, with hypothetical terms. A management agreement runs for twenty years. The owner may terminate if, for two consecutive years, the hotel fails a performance test: GOP below 90 percent of the approved budget and RevPAR index below 95. In year 4, GOP is $1,900,000 against a budget of $2,200,000, which is about 86 percent, failing the first limb. The RevPAR index is 97, passing the second. Because the test requires both failures, the owner cannot terminate, even though profit is 14 percent short of budget. A test requiring either failure would have allowed termination. One word, “and” instead of “or”, decides whether the owner can replace an underperforming operator. Performance test levels are commercial terms negotiated in each agreement.

Say that out loud now.

Apart-hotels, condo-hotels and the securities question

Some developers sell hotel rooms or serviced apartments as individual condominium units and offer buyers a place in a rental programme run by an operator, sharing the income. Worked example two, hypothetical: a buyer pays $300,000 for a unit, and the programme splits net room revenue 50 percent to the owner and 50 percent to the operator. If the unit earns $40,000 of net room revenue, the owner receives $20,000, a 6.7 percent gross return before the owner’s own costs. In concept, when a buyer is sold a unit mainly for a share of profits from an enterprise someone else manages, securities law may treat the arrangement as an investment contract, with registration or exemption requirements and limits on how it can be marketed. Whether that applies depends on the facts and the jurisdiction. Professional sign-off required: a securities lawyer, before any condo-hotel or rental-pool product is marketed.

Building code classification matters too. Under the International Building Code, transient lodging such as hotels generally falls in a different residential occupancy group from apartments, which can change requirements for fire protection and egress; verify against the current adopted edition. A building designed as apartments and operated as short stays may not meet the code for its actual use.

Two Systems

A conceptual comparison of how Canada and Guyana approach these instruments; verify against primary source before relying on any of it. In Canada, residential tenancies and condominiums are governed by provincial law, so the rules on rent increases, deposits and disclosure differ between provinces, and some cities add their own short-term rental rules [unverified — confirm independently]. Quebec’s civil law tradition uses the concept of divided co-ownership for what other provinces call condominiums. In Guyana, landlord and tenant matters and strata or condominium-style ownership should be checked against current legislation and the land registration system that applies to the parcel; tourism and hotel licensing may involve a separate tourism authority [unverified — confirm independently]. The principle in both: the legal instrument for each asset type is set by local law, and the same product may be regulated quite differently across a border.

Mixed-use: the shared facilities agreement

When components of a mixed-use building are owned separately, for example a hotel owned by one company and condominium units owned by individual buyers, the parts that serve everyone need an agreement of their own. Often called a shared facilities or reciprocal agreement, it decides who maintains the structure, roof, cores, loading dock and building systems, how the costs are split, who controls access and what happens if one owner stops paying. It is usually registered against title so it binds future owners. Next week you will study the title instruments, such as easements and declarations, that make that possible.

The trap is to draft it last. By the time the building is designed, the cost split has often been decided by the drawings, and the condominium declaration, the hotel management agreement and the lender’s security all assume something about it. Draft the shared facilities principles at the start of design, so the legal structure and the physical building agree. Professional sign-off required: a real estate lawyer for the agreement and its registration.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is choosing a product, especially a hybrid, without confirming which instruments govern it and what they make mandatory. The control: before design is fixed, get a short written memo from counsel on the tenancy, condominium, hotel, securities and code classification rules that apply to the chosen product.

The beginner’s mistake

The beginner signs the brand’s standard management agreement because the brand is famous. The professional negotiates the term, the performance test, the owner’s budget approval and the cost of terminating, because those clauses decide who controls the asset for twenty years.

Callback

In Week 20 you learned that a contract’s conditions and remedies decide what happens when things go wrong. A hotel management agreement’s performance test is exactly that: a condition with a remedy, and the conjunction between its limbs decides whether the remedy ever becomes available. In Week 21 you met agency; a hotel operator is your agent, binding you to staff contracts and suppliers in your name.

Recap

Rentals sit under tenancy law, condominiums under a statute and a declaration, hotels under a management agreement, and hybrids under several, possibly including securities law. Much of this is mandatory. Read the instruments, get a written memo and negotiate the clauses that decide control.

Next: Nadia, The Numbers — a full hotel and an apart-hotel worked from room nights to value.
checklist: Get a written memo from counsel on every instrument governing the chosen product.
Treat tenancy and condominium protections as fixed parameters, not negotiable terms.
Read a management agreement’s performance test for “and” versus “or”.
Negotiate term, budget approval and termination cost before signing with an operator.
Get securities advice before marketing any rental-pool or condo-hotel product.
Confirm the building code occupancy group for the actual use, transient or residential.
Check how each instrument differs across every jurisdiction you operate in.
head: Field checklist
speak: Every asset type is a legal structure first. A rental lives under residential tenancy law, which often overrides the lease. A condominium is created by registering a declaration under a statute that also regulates deposits and disclosure. A hotel usually runs under a management agreement, where the operator runs the hotel in my name and at my cost, for fees. Its termination test matters most. On hypothetical terms, if I can terminate only when profit is below 90 percent of budget and the RevPAR index is below 95, a hotel 14 percent short on profit with an index of 97 cannot be terminated. The word and instead of or decides who controls my asset. A condo-hotel rental programme may also be treated as a security, so it needs a securities lawyer before marketing. In Canada these rules are provincial; in Guyana they must be checked against current law. I read the instruments before I choose the product.
terms: Hotel management agreement — a contract under which an operator runs a hotel for the owner, at the owner’s cost, for fees.
Condominium declaration — the registered document that creates a condominium, defining units, common elements and each unit’s share.
Investment contract — in concept, an arrangement where people invest money expecting profits from others’ efforts, which securities law may regulate.

hostile.q: Your operator has missed budget three years running. Why can’t you replace them?
hostile.a: Because the performance test requires both a profit shortfall and a RevPAR index below 95, and their index is 97. On the next hotel, the test is either limb, the budget approval is ours, and termination without cause carries a fixed fee we have priced.

title: Room nights to value: a hotel and an apart-hotel, step by step
summary: A hypothetical 120-room hotel and a 120-suite apart-hotel are worked from room nights to net operating income and value. The hotel has the higher RevPAR, about 115 dollars against about 107, but the apart-hotel’s lighter costs give it the higher NOI, about 1.39 million against 1.29 million. RevPAR measures the top line, not the result.
body:
Mr Shabazz, today we work two hospitality assets from the first number to the last: room nights available, through revenue, profit, fees and reserves, to value. The one with the better headline metric does not win.

Recall

Q. From this week, what single word can decide whether an owner can terminate a hotel operator?

A. Whether the performance test joins its limbs with “and” or “or”. With “and”, the operator must fail both tests before the owner can act.

Q. From cycles, what is the break-even exit cap rate?

A. The exit cap rate at which net sale proceeds just equal total cost; compare it with the worst year of the last cycle.

Q. From liability, why do developers hold each project in a separate company?

A. To ring-fence liabilities, so that a failure in one project does not reach the assets of the others, provided the separation is real and respected.

Why this matters

Nadia here. Hospitality numbers are full of percentages and ratios that sound precise and hide the units. If you do not know whether a figure is per room, per night, per available room or per occupied room, you cannot check it. Today every line carries its unit. All figures are hypothetical, and fee and reserve percentages are commercial practice set in each agreement, not standards.

Worked example one: a 120-room hotel

  1. Room nights available. 120 rooms times 365 nights is 43,800 room nights a year.
  2. Room nights sold. At 72 percent occupancy, 43,800 times 0.72 is 31,536 room nights.
  3. Rooms revenue. At an average daily rate (ADR) of $160, 31,536 times $160 is $5,045,760.
  4. Revenue per available room (RevPAR). $5,045,760 divided by 43,800 is $115.20. Check: $160 times 0.72 is also $115.20.
  5. Total revenue. Rooms are 80 percent of revenue; food, beverage and other income make up the rest. $5,045,760 divided by 0.80 is $6,307,200.
  6. Gross operating profit (GOP). At a 35 percent margin, $6,307,200 times 0.35 is $2,207,520.
  7. Base management fee. 3 percent of total revenue: $189,216.
  8. Incentive fee. 8 percent of GOP: $176,602.
  9. Fixed charges. Property tax and insurance: $300,000.
  10. FF&E reserve. 4 percent of total revenue: $252,288.
  11. Net operating income (NOI). $2,207,520 minus $189,216, $176,602, $300,000 and $252,288 is about $1,289,400.
  12. Value. At an 8.5 percent cap rate, $1,289,400 divided by 0.085 is about $15,170,000, or about $126,400 per room.

Say that out loud now.

Worked example two: a 120-suite apart-hotel

Same land, same number of keys, a different business. Suites are larger with kitchens, guests stay longer, there is no full restaurant and staffing is lighter.

  1. Room nights available. 43,800, as before.
  2. Room nights sold. At 82 percent occupancy, 35,916.
  3. Rooms revenue. At an ADR of $130, 35,916 times $130 is $4,669,080.
  4. RevPAR. $4,669,080 divided by 43,800 is about $106.60, lower than the hotel’s $115.20.
  5. Total revenue. Rooms are 95 percent of revenue: $4,669,080 divided by 0.95 is about $4,914,800.
  6. GOP. At a 45 percent margin, about $2,211,700, almost the same as the hotel’s, on much less revenue.
  7. Base fee at 3 percent of revenue, about $147,400. Incentive fee at 8 percent of GOP, about $176,900. Fixed charges, $300,000. FF&E reserve at 4 percent of revenue, about $196,600.
  8. NOI. About $1,390,700, roughly $100,000 more than the hotel.
  9. Value. At the same 8.5 percent cap rate, about $16,360,000. If buyers see the longer stays as more stable and apply 8.0 percent, about $17,380,000.

Reading the result

The hotel wins on RevPAR by about $8.60 a night. The apart-hotel wins on NOI by about $100,000 a year and on value by more than $1,000,000. RevPAR is a measure of how well rooms are sold; it says nothing about what it costs to sell them. That is why hotel professionals also look at GOP per available room, often abbreviated GOPPAR: GOP divided by room nights available. Here the hotel’s GOPPAR is $2,207,520 divided by 43,800, about $50.40, and the apart-hotel’s is about $50.50. Nearly identical profit per available room, from very different revenue.

The sensitivity that matters

Hotels carry more operating leverage, because many of their costs are fixed. Suppose occupancy at the hotel falls from 72 to 62 percent in a downturn, with ADR unchanged. Rooms revenue falls by about 14 percent, to about $4,345,000, and total revenue to about $5,431,000. If costs are largely fixed, GOP might fall far more than 14 percent, because most of the lost revenue was profit. Test that case in the pro forma before you choose the product, because it is the case the lender will test.

Worked example three: the hotel in a downturn

Operating leverage needs a number. Return to the hotel in worked example one. Its operating costs are total revenue minus GOP: $6,307,200 minus $2,207,520, which is $4,099,680. Assume, hypothetically, that 60 percent of those costs are fixed in the short run, about $2,459,800, and the rest vary with revenue at about 26 cents per dollar.

  1. Downturn revenue. Occupancy falls from 72 to 62 percent at the same ADR: 43,800 times 0.62 times $160 is about $4,345,000 of rooms revenue, and total revenue at 80 percent rooms is about $5,431,200, down about 14 percent.
  2. Costs. Fixed costs stay at about $2,459,800. Variable costs are 0.26 times $5,431,200, about $1,412,100.
  3. GOP. $5,431,200 minus $2,459,800 minus $1,412,100 is about $1,559,300, down about 29 percent.
  4. Below GOP. Base fee at 3 percent, about $162,900; incentive fee at 8 percent of GOP, about $124,700; fixed charges $300,000; FF&E reserve at 4 percent, about $217,200.
  5. NOI. About $754,400, down about 42 percent from $1,289,400.

A 14 percent fall in revenue became a 42 percent fall in NOI. If the loan’s annual payments were $900,000, coverage has gone from about 1.43 to about 0.84: the hotel no longer pays its debt from its own income. That is the case the lender will run, and it is why hotels get less leverage than apartments.

Checking a hotel number in your head

Three quick checks catch most errors in a hotel pro forma before you open the spreadsheet. First, RevPAR must be lower than ADR, because occupancy is below 100 percent; if they are equal, someone left occupancy out. Second, annual rooms revenue divided by the number of rooms divided by 365 should equal RevPAR; on the hotel above, $5,045,760 divided by 120 divided by 365 is $115.20, which matches. Third, NOI as a share of total revenue for a full-service hotel is usually well below the share for an apartment building, here about 20 percent, against about 64 percent in this week’s rental example. If a hotel pro forma shows NOI close to half of revenue, find out which deductions are missing before you believe it.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is choosing a hospitality product on RevPAR or ADR alone. The control: carry every option through to NOI with its own margin, fees and reserve, and compare GOPPAR and value side by side, including a downturn case.

The beginner’s mistake

The beginner multiplies ADR by the number of rooms and by 365, forgetting occupancy, and presents a revenue figure about 40 percent too high. Always write the unit: per room night sold, or per room night available.

Callback

In Week 11 you learned that cash and profit are different; here, the FF&E reserve is cash set aside before it is spent, which is why it sits above the NOI line. And in Week 15, the equity multiple taught you to measure what comes back on what goes in; the apart-hotel produces more value on similar capital, so it would also produce the better multiple.

Recap

Work hospitality from room nights available to NOI, writing the unit on every line. On these numbers the hotel had the higher RevPAR and the apart-hotel the higher NOI and value. Compare GOPPAR and test a downturn, because hotels carry high operating leverage.

Next: Remi, The Room — the meeting where a hotel brand pitches you its numbers.
checklist: Start every hospitality model from room nights available.
Write the unit on every line: per room night sold or per room night available.
Check RevPAR two ways: rooms revenue over nights available, and ADR times occupancy.
Deduct base fee, incentive fee, fixed charges and FF&E reserve before NOI.
Compare options on GOPPAR, NOI and value, not on RevPAR alone.
Run a downturn case with occupancy at least 10 points lower.
Use the cap rate buyers actually apply to each product.
head: Field checklist
speak: I worked two hypothetical assets from room nights to value. A 120-room hotel has 43,800 room nights a year. At 72 percent occupancy and a 160-dollar rate, rooms revenue is about 5.05 million and RevPAR is 115.20. Total revenue is about 6.3 million, gross operating profit at 35 percent is about 2.2 million, and after a 3 percent base fee, an 8 percent incentive fee, 300,000 of fixed charges and a 4 percent furniture reserve, NOI is about 1.29 million, worth about 15.2 million at 8.5 percent. A 120-suite apart-hotel at 82 percent and 130 dollars has a lower RevPAR, about 106.60, but at a 45 percent margin its NOI is about 1.39 million and its value about 16.4 million. Profit per available room is almost identical. RevPAR measures how well rooms sell, not what it costs to sell them.
terms: Room night — one room occupied, or available, for one night; the basic unit of hotel accounting.
GOPPAR — gross operating profit divided by room nights available.
Operating leverage — the degree to which fixed costs make profit fall faster than revenue when demand drops.

hostile.q: Your hotel’s RevPAR beats the apart-hotel’s. Why would you build the apart-hotel?
hostile.a: Because RevPAR stops at the top line. After operating costs, fees and the reserve, the apart-hotel earns about 100,000 more NOI on the same land and keys, its profit per available room is the same, and its lighter fixed costs make it fall less in a downturn.

title: The brand pitch: when the operator brings the numbers
summary: A hotel brand’s development team arrives with an impressive projection and a standard management agreement. The question behind the question is how much control and fee they can secure for how long. Ask for their actual performance in comparable hotels, separate the brand’s projection from your underwriting, and negotiate the clauses that decide control.
body:
Mr Shabazz, when a hotel brand pitches you, the projection on the screen is a sales document, and the agreement in the folder is the real offer. Your job in the room is to admire the first politely and negotiate the second seriously.

Recall

Q. From this week, what is GOPPAR, and why look at it?

A. Gross operating profit per available room night. It shows profit per room, not just revenue, so it reveals when a higher RevPAR comes with higher costs.

Q. From cycles, how should you treat a broker’s deadline?

A. As a negotiating tactic until it is in writing from the seller, and never waive conditions in the same meeting.

Q. From liability, what does an agent’s authority mean for the principal?

A. The principal can be bound by contracts the agent makes within its authority, and sometimes by those that appear to be within it.

Why this matters

Remi here. A strong brand can raise a hotel’s room rate, fill it through a reservation system and make it easier to finance. Those benefits are real. But the brand’s development team is paid to sign hotels, and the agreement they bring is drafted to protect the brand’s fees for decades. The meeting decides how much of your asset you hand to someone else, and on what terms you can take it back.

The scene

This is a composite example. You are considering a 150-room hotel on a site you control. A brand’s development director presents: ADR of $190 and occupancy of 78 percent by year three, RevPAR of about $148, “supported by our system’s strength”. She hands you a standard management agreement with a 25-year term, a base fee of 3 percent of revenue, an incentive fee, a performance test that requires two failures together, and a requirement to refurbish to brand standards every seven years at your cost. Your independent market study shows ADR of $165 and occupancy of 70 percent, RevPAR of about $116.

The question behind the question

She is not really asking whether you like the projection. She is asking how much control and fee income the brand can secure for how long, and whether you will sign without reading. There is often a second question: does this owner understand hotels, or can the brand set the budget unopposed for twenty-five years? Your questions in the first ten minutes answer that for her.

Lines to say

  • “Thank you. Before we discuss your projection, can you share the actual RevPAR index of your three nearest comparable hotels over the last five years?”
  • “We underwrite to our independent study: $165 and 70 percent. If your system delivers more, that is upside we will share through the incentive fee.”
  • “The performance test needs to be either limb, not both, and measured against a competitive set we agree now.”
  • “We need approval of the annual budget and of the general manager, and a fixed termination fee if we sell or end the agreement without cause.”
  • “Twenty-five years is long. What would you need to accept fifteen with a renewal at our option?”

Say that out loud now.

The worked numbers behind your lines

All figures are hypothetical. At the brand’s projection, 150 rooms times 365 nights times $148 RevPAR is about $8,100,000 of rooms revenue. At your study’s $116 it is about $6,350,000, a gap of about $1,750,000 a year. If you sized the loan on the brand’s number, your coverage would be built on revenue that has not been earned. Separately, on hypothetical total revenue of $8,000,000, a 3 percent base fee is $240,000 a year, about $6,000,000 over 25 years before any incentive fee, payable whether or not the hotel makes money. The term and the termination clause decide how much of that you could ever avoid.

Lines never to say

  • “Your numbers look great.” You have just adopted their projection as yours.
  • “We’ll have our lawyer look at it later.” It tells her the commercial terms are settled.
  • “We don’t really know hotels.” She will believe you and draft accordingly.
  • “Can you reduce your fee?” as the first ask. Fees matter less than control; start with the performance test and the budget.

When to stay silent

After you ask for actual RevPAR index of comparable hotels, wait. If the answer is vague, or limited to the hotels that perform best, that silence has told you what you needed. Do not fill it with reassurance.

Holding your state

Brand presentations are designed to make an owner feel chosen. Notice the pull to agree with a polished team that is flattering your site. Keep your independent study on the table, open at the ADR page, and bring every conversation back to it. Professional sign-off required: a lawyer experienced in hotel management agreements before you sign anything, including a letter of intent with exclusivity.

If she pushes back

She may say: “The performance test is our standard; every owner signs it.” Answer with structure, not irritation: “I understand it is your starting point. Our lender will ask what we can do if the hotel underperforms its competitive set for two years. With a test requiring both limbs, the answer is nothing, and that affects how much they will lend. Help me give them a better answer.” You have turned the clause from your preference into the lender’s requirement, which is usually true and is harder for a brand to refuse.

She may also say the brand needs a long term to justify its investment in your hotel. Ask what that investment is in dollars. If the brand is contributing key money, a sum paid to the owner to win the agreement, a longer term may be fair. If it is contributing nothing but its name, the term is a request, not a cost recovery.

Fees beyond the fee

The base and incentive fees are only part of what the brand is paid. Ask for a full schedule of system charges: reservation and distribution fees, loyalty programme charges, marketing contributions, technology fees and any centralised services charged back to the hotel. Each is commercial practice that varies by brand and agreement. Add them up as a percentage of revenue for a stabilised year. The total is the real cost of the brand, and it belongs beside the rate premium the brand claims to deliver.

The letter of intent trap

Brands often ask an owner to sign a letter of intent before the full agreement is negotiated. Most of it may be non-binding, but exclusivity and the key commercial terms are often presented as agreed. Once you sign, you lose the competing brand that gave you leverage, and the main terms are hard to reopen. Negotiate the performance test, term and termination in the letter itself, or keep two brands in discussion until the full agreement is settled.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is accepting the brand’s projection as your underwriting and the brand’s standard agreement as your contract. The control: underwrite to an independent study, and negotiate the performance test, budget approval, term and termination before price and fees.

The beginner’s mistake

The beginner negotiates the fee percentage and signs the rest. The professional knows the fee is visible and the control clauses are where the value sits.

Callback

In Week 25 you learned that an adviser’s incentive leans their advice; a brand’s development team is the same, paid to sign. In Week 5 you learned bottom line first: open the meeting with the one question that matters, actual performance of comparable hotels, before the slides start.

Recap

The brand’s projection is a sales document; the agreement is the offer. Ask for actual comparable performance, underwrite to your own study, and negotiate the performance test, budget approval, term and termination. Stay silent after the hard question.

Next: Kema, Quiz & Recap — six questions on asset types, a Red Pen drill on a hotel pro forma and the boardroom drill.
checklist: Ask for the actual RevPAR index of the brand’s nearest comparable hotels.
Underwrite to an independent market study, never to the brand’s projection.
Negotiate the performance test to either limb, against an agreed competitive set.
Secure owner approval of the annual budget and the general manager.
Negotiate term, renewal at your option and a fixed termination fee.
Price the brand’s refurbishment requirements into the long-term budget.
Get a hotel agreement lawyer before signing any exclusive letter of intent.
head: Field checklist
speak: A brand’s development team shows me a projection and a standard management agreement. The projection is a sales document; the agreement is the real offer. The question behind the question is how much control and fee they can lock in for how long. So my first question is the actual RevPAR index of their three nearest comparable hotels over five years. On hypothetical numbers, their projection of 148 dollars RevPAR against my study’s 116 is about 1.75 million of rooms revenue a year on 150 rooms, so I underwrite to my study and treat anything better as upside. A 3 percent base fee on 8 million of revenue is about 6 million over 25 years, so the control clauses matter more than the fee: a performance test on either limb, owner approval of the budget and general manager, a shorter term and a fixed termination fee. After the hard question, I stay silent.
terms: Brand standards — the operating, design and refurbishment requirements a hotel brand imposes on the owner, at the owner’s cost.
Competitive set — the group of nearby comparable hotels against which a hotel’s performance is measured.
Termination fee — a fixed or formula amount an owner pays to end a management agreement early without cause.

hostile.q: Our system will deliver a 20 percent rate premium. Why won’t you underwrite to it?
hostile.a: Show me the RevPAR index of your three nearest comparable hotels over five years and I will consider it. Until then, the loan is sized on our independent study, and any premium you deliver flows through your incentive fee, so you are paid for exactly what you achieve.

role: Chief of staff and learning coach
title: Asset types week: quiz, recap and the Red Pen
summary: Six questions test the four asset types, RevPAR, Rule 29, the hotel chain to NOI, the management agreement’s performance test and GOPPAR. The Red Pen drill finds the planted defects in a hypothetical hotel pro forma, and the boardroom drill explains asset types in two minutes.
body:
Mr Shabazz, this week showed that one building can be several businesses, each with its own metrics, legal instrument, lender and buyer, and that the biggest revenue often produces the smallest value. Today you test it, then mark up a hotel pro forma that forgot it.

Recall

Q. From this week, what should you ask a hotel brand before discussing its projection?

A. For the actual RevPAR index of its nearest comparable hotels over several years.

Q. From cycles, why set the exit cap rate above today’s?

A. Because the cycle may be at a different point on the day you sell, and assuming today’s pricing at exit assumes the cycle stands still.

Q. From liability, what makes ring-fencing in separate companies work?

A. Real separation: separate accounts, documents and decisions, and no cross-guarantees that link the companies’ liabilities.

The six questions

Question 1. How does a condominium earn its money differently from a rental? Answer: A condominium earns a one-time profit when units are sold and closed, then the developer leaves. A rental earns lease income for as long as it is owned and is valued on net operating income.

Question 2. A hotel has an ADR of $150 and occupancy of 70 percent. What is its RevPAR? Answer: $150 times 0.70, which is $105.

Question 3. What was the root cause at Stuyvesant Town, and what is Rule 29? Answer: Debt sized on income the rules did not yet allow. Rule 29: underwrite the income the asset type and its rules allow today, and never size debt on income you can only earn by changing the tenants, the law or the market.

Question 4. What comes off a hotel’s gross operating profit before NOI? Answer: The base management fee, any incentive fee, fixed charges such as property tax and insurance, and the FF&E reserve.

Question 5. Why does “and” versus “or” matter in a management agreement’s performance test? Answer: With “and”, the operator must fail every limb before the owner can terminate; with “or”, failing one is enough. The conjunction decides who controls the asset.

Question 6. What is GOPPAR, and what does it show that RevPAR does not? Answer: Gross operating profit per available room night. It shows profit, so it reveals whether a higher RevPAR came with higher costs.

Recap

Rentals earn rent and are valued on NOI at relatively low cap rates. Condominiums earn profit once. Hotels are operating businesses measured by ADR, occupancy, RevPAR and GOP, and they pay fees, fixed charges and a furniture reserve before reaching NOI, which buyers value at higher cap rates. Each type rests on a different legal instrument. Underwrite the income the rules allow today.

Say that out loud now.

Red Pen

Read this hypothetical extract from a hotel pro forma summary and find the defects before reading the list.

Hotel pro forma summary, hypothetical. 150 rooms. ADR $190, per the brand’s projection. Year 1 occupancy 82 percent. Rooms revenue: 150 rooms times $190 times 365, $10,402,500. GOP margin 40 percent. NOI equals GOP: $4,161,000. Valued at a 5.5 percent cap rate, consistent with apartment sales in the area: $75,650,000. Loan requested at 70 percent of value.

The defects:

  1. ADR from the brand. The projection is a sales document. Underwrite to an independent study.
  2. Year 1 occupancy of 82 percent. New hotels ramp up over several years; year 1 at a stabilised or above-stabilised level is not credible without evidence.
  3. Occupancy left out of rooms revenue. 150 times $190 times 365 assumes every room sold every night. At 82 percent the figure would be about $8,530,000, and at a realistic year-1 level much less.
  4. Rooms revenue treated as total revenue for the margin. The basis of the GOP margin is not stated.
  5. NOI equals GOP. Management fees, fixed charges and the FF&E reserve are missing.
  6. Apartment cap rate applied to a hotel. Buyers price hotel income at higher cap rates because it is more volatile.
  7. Loan sized on that value. Every error above compounds into the loan request.

Boardroom drill

Explain this week to a board in two minutes. Set a timer, speak, then compare with the model answer.

Model answer: “The asset type is the business we choose. A rental earns lease income and is valued on net operating income at a relatively low cap rate. A condominium earns one profit on sale, fast, if buyers close. A hotel is an operating business: we measure average daily rate, occupancy and revenue per available room, which is the two multiplied, then gross operating profit. Before net operating income, a hotel pays its operator’s fees, its fixed charges and a reserve to replace furniture, and buyers then apply a higher cap rate. So a hotel with twice an apartment building’s revenue can be worth half as much. Each type sits on a different legal instrument: tenancy law, a condominium declaration or a hotel management agreement, whose termination test decides who controls the asset. And from Stuyvesant Town, we underwrite the income the rules allow today, never the income we hope the rules will allow.”

How to score your boardroom drill

Listen back and check five things. Did you open with the bottom line, that the asset type is the business? Did you define RevPAR correctly as average daily rate times occupancy? Did you name the four deductions between gross operating profit and NOI? Did you mention the legal instrument for each type? And did you close with Rule 29? Score a point for each. Four or five means the week is yours; three or fewer, replay Days 3 and 5.

One exercise for this week

Pick one neighbourhood you know, with no project attached, and list every hotel, apart-hotel, rental and condominium building you can find. For each hotel, look for publicly advertised room rates on a weekday and a weekend in high and low season, and note the range. You will start to see how much a nightly business moves compared with monthly rent.

Mistakes to listen for

Listen for three slips that most people make the first time. Saying RevPAR is the rate a hotel charges: it is revenue per available room, which already includes occupancy. Saying a hotel is worth more because it earns more: say instead that it earns more and keeps less. And saying the brand guarantees the performance: brands rarely guarantee anything, and the management agreement usually states that projections are not promises.

A final check on structure. A good two-minute answer has three parts in this order: what each asset type is, how each turns revenue into value, and the rule that protects you. If your answer wandered between hotels and condominiums without that order, record it again and say the three parts aloud before you start.

And a check on composure. When you reach the hotel chain, there are four deductions to name in a row. Say them slowly and count them on your fingers if it helps: fees, incentive fee, fixed charges, reserve. A list spoken at an even pace sounds like knowledge; the same list rushed sounds like memorisation.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk this week is comparing asset types on revenue. Compare them on value, capital, speed of return and downturn behaviour.

The beginner’s mistake

The beginner thinks a famous brand makes a hotel safe. The professional knows the brand fills rooms and the agreement decides whether the owner keeps the profit.

Callback

In Week 28 you learned to count only end-user demand as absorption. Hotels add a twist: demand is measured in room nights, by segment, such as business, leisure and group, and each segment behaves differently in a downturn. A feasibility study for a hotel that does not split demand by segment is the hotel version of counting investors as occupiers.

hostile.q: Why does your hotel valuation use an 8.5 percent cap rate when apartments here trade at 5.5?
hostile.a: Because hotel buyers price income that changes every night and carries operating risk, and the hotel sales we found traded well above apartment cap rates. Using the apartment rate would overstate value by more than half and lead to a loan the hotel’s income cannot carry in a downturn.
